exampleAnswers.title: Expressing the Area Between Two Curves as an Integral Given the Limits of Integration

question.text:
Which integral gives the area of the finite region bounded by $y=2x^2-2$ and $y =1-x^2,$ shown above?

(Note: Figure not drawn to scale)
question.explanation:
The diagram shows that the intersection points between the two graphs occur when $x=-1$ and $x=1.$ So these will be our limits of integration.

To determine which is the lower function and which is the upper, let's draw our vertical arrow.

The vertical line

  • enters the region through the lower function $y=2x^2-2,$ and

  • leaves through the upper function $y = 1-x^2.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our area is

\begin{align*} A &= \int_{-1}^{1}\left[\,\left(\color{brown}{\textrm{upper function}}\right) - \left(\color{blue}{\textrm{lower function}}\right)\,\right]\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{-1}^{1}\left[\,\left(\color{brown}{1-x^2}\right) - \left(\color{blue}{2x^2-2}\right)\,\right]\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{-1}^{1} \left(-3x^2+3 \right) \textrm{d}x. \end{align*}

question.text:
Which integral gives the area of the finite region bounded by $y=8x^2-5$ and $y= 1-2x,$ shown above?

(Note: Figure not drawn to scale)
question.explanation:
The diagram shows that the intersection points between the two graphs occur when $x=-1$ and $x=\dfrac{3}{4}.$ So these will be our limits of integration.

To determine which is the lower function and which is the upper, let's draw our vertical arrow.

The vertical line

  • enters the region through the lower function $y=8x^2-5,$ and

  • leaves through the upper function $y=1-2x.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our area is

\begin{align*} A &= \int_{-1}^{3/4}\left[\,\left(\color{brown}{\textrm{upper function}}\right) - \left(\color{blue}{\textrm{lower function}}\right)\,\right]\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= \int_{-1}^{3/4}\left[\,\left(\color{brown}{1-2x}\right) - \left(\color{blue}{8x^2-5}\right)\,\right]\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= \int_{-1}^{3/4}\left(-8x^2-2x+6\right)\,\textrm{d}x. \end{align*}

exampleAnswers.title: Expressing the Area Between Two Curves as an Integral by First Solving For the Limits of Integration

question.text:
Which integral gives the area of the finite region bounded between $g(x) = 2-x^2-2x$ and $f(x) = 2x^2+6x-1,$ shown above?

(Note: Figure not drawn to scale)
question.explanation:
First, we want to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we equate the two functions and solve for $x\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} 2-x^2-2x &= 2x^2+6x-1 \\[5pt] 3x^2+8x-3 &= 0 \\[5pt] x &= \dfrac{-8 \pm \sqrt{8^2 - 4 \cdot 3 \cdot (-3)}}{2\cdot3} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{-8 \pm 10}{6} \end{align*}

Hence, we need to integrate from $x=-3$ to $x=\dfrac 1 3.$

To determine which is the lower function and which is the upper, we draw our vertical arrow.

The vertical line

  • enters the region through the lower function $y=2x^2+6x-1,$ and

  • leaves through the upper function $y=2-x^2-2x.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our area is

\begin{align*} A &= \int_{-3}^{1/3}\left[\,\left(\color{brown}{\textrm{upper function}}\right) - \left(\color{blue}{\textrm{lower function}}\right)\,\right]\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= \int_{-3}^{1/3} \left[\, ({\color{brown}2-x^2-2x}) - ({\color{blue}2x^2+6x-1}) \,\right] \:\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{-3}^{1/3} (-3x^2-8x+3) \:\textrm{d}x. \end{align*}

question.text: Which integral gives the area of the finite region bounded between $y = x^2-4x+3 $ and $y =x-1?$
question.explanation:
First, let's draw a sketch of the two functions.

(Note: Figure not drawn to scale)

Now, we want to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we equate the two functions and solve for $x\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} x^2-4x+3 &= x-1 \\[5pt] x^2-5x+4 &= 0 \\[5pt] (x-1)(x-4) &= 0 \end{align*}

Hence, we need to integrate from $x=1$ to $x=4.$

To determine which is the lower function and which is the upper, let's draw our vertical arrow.

The vertical line

  • enters the region through the lower function $y=x^2-4x+3,$ and

  • leaves through the upper function $y=x-1.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our area is

\begin{align*} A &= \int_{1}^{4} \left[\,\left(\color{brown}{\textrm{upper function}}\right) - \left(\color{blue}{\textrm{lower function}}\right)\,\right] \,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= \int_{1}^{4} \left[\, \left(x-1\right) - \left(x^2-4x+3\right) \,\right] \, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{1}^{4} \left( -x^2+5x-4 \right) \, \textrm{d}x. \end{align*}

exampleAnswers.title: Calculating the Area Between Two Curves Expressed as Functions of X

question.text:
Find the area $A$ of the finite region enclosed between $y =-3x^2+8 $ and $y = -x^2,$ shown above. Do not round the answer.

(Note: Figure not drawn to scale)
question.explanation:
First, we want to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we equate the two functions and solve for $x{:}$ \begin{align*} -3x^2+8 &= -x^2 \\[5pt] -2x^2+8 &= 0 \\[5pt] x^2-4 &= 0 \\[5pt] (x - 2)(x+2) &= 0 \end{align*}

Hence, we need to integrate from $x=-2$ to $x=2.$

To determine which is the lower function and which is the upper, let's draw our vertical arrow.

The vertical line

  • enters the region through the lower function $y=-x^2,$ and

  • leaves through the upper function $y=-3x^2+8.$

We can now set up the integration with our $x$ values (Top-Bottom): \begin{align*} A &=\int_{-2}^{2}\left[\,\left(\color{blue}{\textrm{upper function}}\right) - \left(\color{brown}{\textrm{lower function}}\right) \,\right]\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= \int_{-2}^{2} \left[ ({\color{blue}-3x^2+8}) - ({\color{brown}-x^2}) \,\right]\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{-2}^{2} \left( -2x^2+8 \right) \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{-2}^{2} \left( 8-2x^2 \right) \textrm{d}x \end{align*}

Notice that the integrand is an even function. Therefore, we can find the area as follows: \begin{align*} A &= 2\int_{0}^{2} \left( 8-2x^2 \right) \, \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= 2\left.\left(8x - \dfrac{2}{3}x^3\right)\right|_0^2\\[5pt] &=2\left(\left(8\cdot2 - \dfrac{2}{3}\cdot 2^3\right)-0\right)\\[5pt] &=2\left(\left(16 - \dfrac{16}{3}\right)-\left(0\right)\right)\\[5pt] &=2\cdot\dfrac{32}{3}\\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{64}{3}}. \end{align*}

example.title: Calculating the Area Between Two Curves Expressed as Functions of X

question.text: Calculate the area of the finite region bounded by the curves $y=-x^2-2 $ and $y=-x-2.$
question.explanation:
First, let's draw a sketch:

(Note: Figure not drawn to scale)

Now, we want to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we equate the two functions and solve for $x\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} -x^2-2 &= -x-2 \\[3pt] x-x^2 &= 0 \\[3pt] x(1-x) &= 0 \end{align*}

Hence, we need to integrate from $x=0$ to $x=1.$

To determine which is the lower function and which is the upper, we draw our vertical arrow.

The vertical line

  • enters the region through the lower function $y=-x-2,$ and

  • leaves through the upper function $y=-x^2-2.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our area is

\begin{align*} A &=\int_{0}^{1}\left[\,\left(\color{blue}{\textrm{upper function}}\right) - \left(\color{brown}{\textrm{lower function}}\right) \,\right]\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{1} \left[\, ({\color{blue}-x^2-2}) - ({\color{brown}-x-2}) \,\right] \:\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{1} (x-x^2) \:\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \left.\left(\dfrac{x^2}{2} - \dfrac{x^3}{3}\right)\right|_{0}^1 \\[5pt] &= \left( \dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac 1 3 \right) - \left( 0 - 0 \right) \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{6} \end{align*}
